rv.q: Jingle those bells joyfully: here is a real Christmas cracker from the National Theatre, one whose pleasures will surely be enjoyed for myriad festive seasons to come.
This delicious show about three female foundlings forging their own identities, and a makeshift family, in a house full of oddballs in interwar London absolutely bowled me over.

Ballet Shoes is as delicately balanced as a dancer en pointe as it leaps between its period setting and the present, finding ways to diversify and complexify this story in ways that never feel lazy or jarring.

Under the direction of Katy Rudd, this is an exquisite Christmas cracker of a show, albeit an elegant one that never quite let its hair down, but still it is filled with spectacular theatricality and fabulous performances all round.
What you get here is a beguiling play with music that exemplifies the very best of the National’s production values.
It’s still a loveable, big-hearted production that captures imaginations and tickles the humour of audiences of all ages.
It’s a Christmas show with heart, soul and a flurry of movement to sweep you away.

This new adaptation by Kendall Feaver hits the sweet spot, thankfully retaining the 1930s setting and celebrating what a visionary Streatfeild was with her focus on young women shaping their own destinies, the importance of technique and hard graft, and the gift of found families.

cn.t: Critics hail this National Theatre adaptation as a gorgeous, gutsy Christmas offering that skillfully modernizes Streatfeild's beloved novel. Feaver's adaptation and Rudd's direction win widespread praise for their delicate mastery and stellar production values.
